island-park.summary: Island Park splits between the City of Island Park (a famously narrow ~500-foot-wide, 33-mile-long strip) and unincorporated Fremont County, which covers nearly all of the Henry's Lake and Island Park Reservoir subdivision corridor. Idaho HB 583 (effective July 1, 2026) now bars both governments from requiring an STR-specific license, permit, fee, or registration, from capping STR counts, and from mandating owner-occupancy — the county's old $200/$500 Class 1/2 lodging-permit program is no longer legally enforceable, though its application materials may still be nominally posted. The one confirmed, real constraint is private: a Fremont County HOA can still enforce a pre-existing rental ban, as the Idaho Supreme Court just confirmed in a case decided in this exact area.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No, as of July 1, 2026 — Fremont County's former Home Occupation Transient Rental Permit (Class 1: up to 15 guests, $200/yr; Class 2: 16–30 guests, $500/yr, both with biennial septic/well inspections) is no longer a legally enforceable precondition to operate. The county's own application/renewal PDFs may still be posted online; treat them as stale, not current law, and confirm directly with Fremont County Planning & Building before assuming any fee is still owed. No dedicated city-level STR ordinance was found for Island Park distinct from the county's.
Primary residence required? No — owner-occupancy mandates are barred statewide, and none was found pre-HB 583 either.
operatingLimits: No caps, quotas, or day-limit restrictions — all barred by state law. Occupancy defaults to generally-applicable International Building Code limits. Septic and well inspections remain a real, separate diligence item: Idaho's statewide septic design standard sizes tanks by bedroom count, not by the large group sizes some lake-corridor properties actually market and host, and this is unrelated to (and unaffected by) HB 583's STR-permit preemption.

Taxes: 6% Idaho sales tax + 2% state Travel & Convention Tax = 8% total. No local-option or auditorium-district tax applies — Island Park does not appear on Idaho's resort-city local-option-tax list, and Fremont County has none either.
investorNotes: Idaho Code §67-6539 (as amended by HB 583) bars STR-specific licenses, fees, permits, caps, and owner-occupancy mandates statewide — it does not touch generally-applicable septic, well, zoning, or building-code rules, which still fully apply.

A specific Henry's Lake-area HOA ban was just litigated and upheld in North Henry's Lake HOA v. Norton (Idaho Supreme Court, Jan. 2026): a pre-2016 rental ban survives against non-consenting owners under Idaho Code §55-3211, but a subsequent owner who never consented can still win the right to operate — check the specific subdivision's CC&R and consent history, not just jurisdiction, before assuming legality.

Confirm which side of the city/county line a specific parcel sits on before relying on either code — both now land on the same permissive state-law answer for STR legality, but zoning specifics can still differ.
Airbnb/Vrbo auto-collect and remit state taxes on platform bookings; direct-booking hosts must register with the Idaho State Tax Commission and self-file monthly (Form 1152).

teton-valley.summary: Driggs, Victor, and Tetonia all opposed HB 583 through the Idaho Resort Cities Coalition, and 2.5 months after the law's July 1, 2026 effective date, Driggs and Victor still publicly display and appear to be collecting fees under now-preempted STR permit and business-license programs — a real gap between the law on the books and what's actually enforced on the ground. Unincorporated Teton County is murkier still: the county's own FAQ says it has no STR zoning requirements at all, while independent secondary sources describe a much more built-out registration and septic-based occupancy-cap system in its Land Development Code that could not be verified against primary text.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? On paper, no, as of July 1, 2026. In practice, Driggs' website still shows an $80 initial/$50 annual STR permit with mandatory Fire Marshal and Building Inspector inspection, and Victor's site still shows a $100/$50 per-property Business License — both appear directly barred by Idaho Code §67-6539(5), and neither city has updated its published materials. Tetonia has no STR-specific ordinance found at all. Unincorporated Teton County's own FAQ says it has no zoning requirements for short- or long-term rentals (except campgrounds/B&Bs), which conflicts with secondary-source descriptions of a county STR registration and septic-capacity permit system — unresolved, verify directly with Teton County Planning & Zoning.
Primary residence required? No, anywhere in the valley — barred statewide regardless of what any city website currently displays.
operatingLimits: Driggs' RV/tent/temporary-shelter ban for STR use is still posted and its legal status post-HB 583 is genuinely unresolved. Any occupancy cap tied to septic capacity (as opposed to generic IBC-based limits) in unincorporated Teton County is very likely preempted, but this could not be confirmed against the county's own Land Development Code text.

Taxes: state 8% baseline. Driggs and Victor both raised their lodging local-option tax to 8% (from 6%) in 2025–2026 ballot measures — roughly 16% combined in both cities. Tetonia adopted its first-ever 5% lodging tax effective Jan. 2026 — roughly 13% combined. Unincorporated Teton County has no local-option tax at all — roughly 8% total, a meaningful gap from the three cities.
investorNotes: Idaho Code §67-6539 (HB 583) bars STR-specific licenses, fees, permits, caps, and owner-occupancy mandates statewide, with no population threshold — Driggs and Victor's still-posted fee schedules are very likely legally unenforceable today, but the cities' active political opposition (both mayors publicly fought the law) makes this a live compliance gap worth confirming directly before assuming a fee-free path.

Grand Targhee Resort's actual base area sits in Alta, Wyoming, not Idaho — only the Idaho-side access corridor and any Idaho-side cabins fall under Teton County, ID rules; verify exact parcel jurisdiction via county GIS before assuming a 'Targhee-area' listing is Idaho-regulated.

Idaho Code §55-3211 grandfathers pre-existing HOA rental bans (written consent required for new ones) — Teton Springs and other golf/resort subdivisions may carry their own STR restrictions independent of the permissive state law.

This region's local governments were the most vocal statewide opponents of HB 583 — treat it as more likely than other regions to see future litigation, further legislation, or continued informal non-enforcement disputes.

mccall-west-central-mountains.summary: McCall — historically the region's most restrictive jurisdiction, with a detailed permit, occupancy-formula, and inspection regime — formally repealed its equivalent STR provisions via Ordinance 1038 on July 2, 2026, one day after Idaho HB 583 took effect. Donnelly and unincorporated Valley County never adopted a comparably strict regime and appear not to have yet issued a formal HB-583 conformance ordinance, but state preemption applies regardless of whether local code text has caught up. Cascade's STR-specific rules could not be confirmed from its inaccessible code, though a business-license/tax-permit process clearly exists there.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No, as of July 1, 2026, confirmed formally in McCall via City Council Ordinance 1038 (July 2, 2026), which repealed the city's STR-specific occupancy limits, conditional-use permitting, ADU owner-occupancy rule, and mandatory pre-license inspection. McCall's own STR webpage still lags this ordinance and describes the old rules in future tense — treat the ordinance, not the webpage, as authoritative. Donnelly's code (Ch. 18.85) and Valley County's code (§9-4-10) still describe a permit/conditional-use process on paper, with no confirmed 2026 conformance amendment found for either — both are very likely unenforceable now regardless, but verify directly given the lack of formal repeal.

Primary residence required? No, anywhere in the region — McCall's ADU-specific owner-occupancy rule was expressly repealed by Ordinance 1038, and none of the other three jurisdictions ever required it.
operatingLimits: McCall's old bedrooms×2+2 occupancy formula with an 11-guest conditional-use trigger is repealed; any occupancy limit McCall keeps must now track the International Building Code instead. No numeric STR cap was ever found in any of the four jurisdictions.

Taxes: state 8% baseline. McCall adds a confirmed 7% Local Option Tax (1% general retail + 6% lodging-specific) — roughly 15% combined, the highest confirmed rate in this region and independently corroborated by two secondary tax guides. Cascade has an active Business License/LOT Permit process but its exact rate is unconfirmed. Donnelly and unincorporated Valley County show no confirmed lodging-specific local tax — only the 8% state baseline is certain for those two.
investorNotes: McCall actually won its own STR-ordinance lawsuit in district court in July 2025 (occupancy limits, parking rules, and inspection standards upheld as reasonable), only to see the legislature substantially moot those same provisions a year later via HB 583 — a reminder that a local litigation win doesn't insulate an ordinance from subsequent state preemption.
A same-named 'Ordinance 2026-02' STR result for 'Town of Cascade' found in some searches belongs to Cascade, Montana, not Cascade, Idaho — a naming trap worth flagging so it isn't miscited elsewhere.

Payette Lake shoreline subdivisions in McCall and Donnelly commonly carry private CC&R rental restrictions entirely unaffected by HB 583 — per-parcel title review remains essential regardless of the favorable state and city law.

Idaho Code §67-6539 bars STR-specific licenses/fees/permits/caps statewide — Donnelly and Valley County's still-published permit requirements are very likely dead letter even without a formal repeal ordinance, but confirm directly with each jurisdiction before assuming a fee-free path.

coeur-dalene.summary: Coeur d'Alene's own annual STR permit ordinance is still fully codified — unchanged since 2017 and untouched by the city's most recent code update, six days after HB 583 took effect — but is very likely legally unenforceable under the new state preemption, and the city's public-facing STR web pages are currently offline entirely. Hayden, Post Falls, Harrison, and unincorporated Kootenai County show no dedicated restrictive STR ordinance at all. A widely-repeated '35-unit cap' claim for this region is a mix-up with Sandpoint, a different city in a different county, and should not be applied here.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? On paper, yes in Coeur d'Alene — an annual, non-transferable, per-dwelling STR permit (due March 1) with an annual self-inspection checklist, unchanged since 2017 and still on the books as of a July 2026 code update. This is very likely unenforceable under Idaho Code §67-6539(5), but the city's own STR web pages currently return 404s, so what the city is telling the public today could not be confirmed — call the Coeur d'Alene Planning Department directly. No dedicated STR ordinance was found for Hayden, Post Falls, Harrison, or unincorporated Kootenai County.

Primary residence required? No, generally. Coeur d'Alene's code still contains an ADU-specific rule requiring the primary home or the ADU to be owner/family-occupied 6+ months/year before the other can operate short-term — explicitly the kind of 'owner occupation' condition HB 583 bars, and likely unenforceable now despite remaining codified.
operatingLimits: Coeur d'Alene has no citywide numeric STR cap — the mayor has publicly confirmed this. (The often-cited '35-unit cap' belongs to Sandpoint, a different city in Bonner County, not this region — don't apply it here.) Coeur d'Alene's own occupancy limit is tied to its municipal 'family' definition rather than a stated IBC figure, a possible point of tension with the state law's IBC-based safe harbor.

Taxes: 8% state baseline (6% sales + 2% Travel & Convention) applies in Coeur d'Alene, Hayden, and Post Falls — all three exceed Idaho's 10,000-population cap for resort-city local-option-tax eligibility, so no local add-on exists or is possible. Harrison, with a population under 300, does levy a confirmed 1% Local Option Tax — roughly 9% total there.
investorNotes: Coeur d'Alene's permit/inspection/ADU rules are pre-HB-583 holdovers that the city has not yet formally repealed — a procedural lag, not necessarily a substantive legal barrier, but its current public-facing pages being offline means the city's actual practice today could not be verified.

Don't confuse the City of Hayden (pop. ~15,500–16,500, no STR ordinance found) with the separate, much smaller City of Hayden Lake (pop. ~624, which does have its own detailed STR permit chapter) — these are two different municipalities.

Lake Coeur d'Alene's gated communities, notably Black Rock and Gozzer Ranch, reportedly carry their own stricter HOA rental restrictions (including boat-slip-use tied to rental status) — entirely independent of, and unaffected by, HB 583's government-only preemption.
Idaho Code §67-6539 bars STR-specific licenses, fees, permits, caps, and owner-occupancy mandates statewide — Coeur d'Alene's own ordinance text simply hasn't caught up to it yet.

boise-foothills-eagle.summary: Boise fully repealed and de-codified its STR license as of May 18, 2026, ahead of the July 1 statewide deadline — its municipal code chapter now reads simply '[RESERVED].' Meridian, Eagle, and unincorporated Ada County show no evidence of ever having adopted a dedicated STR ordinance. The main practical variable in this region isn't regulatory risk but tax geography: the Greater Boise Auditorium District's irregular, non-jurisdictional boundary determines whether a specific property owes a 13% or an 8% total tax rate.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No. Boise's STR license (Title 3, Ch. 22, historically ~$80/yr plus insurance and a local-contact requirement) was formally repealed effective May 18, 2026; the chapter is now officially '[RESERVED]' in the city's own code. No dedicated STR ordinance was found, past or present, for Meridian, Eagle, or unincorporated Ada County.
Primary residence required? No, anywhere in this cluster — barred statewide, and none was found historically either.
operatingLimits: No caps, density limits, or owner-occupancy rules in any of the four jurisdictions — all now barred by Idaho Code §67-6539 regardless. Standard IBC-based occupancy limits apply.

Taxes: 8% state baseline (6% sales + 2% Travel & Convention) everywhere in this cluster, plus a confirmed 5% Greater Boise Auditorium District room tax — 13% total — for any property inside the district's boundary. That boundary runs along old Boise Junior College district lines (roughly Floating Feather Rd north, Lake Hazel Rd south, Eagle Rd west, Warm Springs/Gowen confluence east) and explicitly does not track any city or county line — it covers most of Boise and all of Garden City, but only portions of Meridian and Eagle and some unincorporated Ada County land. Confirm a specific parcel's status directly with the district (208-336-8900) before assuming either rate.
investorNotes: Boise's repeal was explicit and self-described as compliance-driven ('to align with changes in Idaho state law') — this is a genuine, confirmed deregulation, not just an assumption based on the state statute.

Idaho Code §67-6539 bars STR-specific licenses, fees, permits, caps, and owner-occupancy mandates statewide — the Idaho Association of Counties has publicly noted this also removes local governments' main tool for proactively identifying STR properties, so enforcement of the still-allowed safety rules is now essentially complaint-driven everywhere in this cluster.

Idaho Code §55-3211 grandfathers pre-existing HOA rental bans but bars new ones without written owner consent — many older Boise Foothills subdivisions predate the Airbnb era and are unlikely to have STR-restrictive CC&Rs, but newer master-planned Eagle/Foothills communities could have restrictions baked into their original declarations. No specific subdivision-level ban was identified either way — check the Ada County Recorder per property.

The 5-point tax swing (8% vs. 13%) inside vs. outside the Auditorium District is the single most consequential number to verify per-property in this region — it can matter more to net yield than any regulatory question.

sun-valley-wood-river.summary: Ketchum's public-facing rules are stale and openly contradict current law — the city's own site still describes a $504 annual STR permit, mandatory inspections, a 2-night minimum, and a one-STR-per-parcel cap, even though council reportedly passed a repeal ordinance months ago. Hailey never had a general STR permit, but its distinctive ADU rule (only one of a primary home + ADU pair may run short-term, the other must go long-term or owner-occupied) is a real, still-operative constraint that likely survives HB 583 because it offers a long-term-rental alternative rather than mandating owner-occupancy outright. Sun Valley and unincorporated Blaine County show comparatively little documented friction.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? Ketchum's website still shows a $504 permit requiring Fire District inspection approval — reportedly repealed by council action around June 2026, but no updated public page or confirmed final ordinance number was found; treat the fee/inspection regime as legally unenforceable but verify directly before relying on the city's own site. Hailey has no general STR permit; its only mechanism is embedded in its ADU code. Sun Valley's STR permit/license status could not be confirmed against its own current code text. No STR-specific ordinance chapter was found for unincorporated Blaine County.

Primary residence required? No general mandate anywhere in the valley. Hailey's ADU rule requires the other unit on a primary+ADU lot to be either owner-occupied or a long-term rental (31+ days) when one unit runs short-term — not a strict owner-occupancy mandate, and likely survives HB 583 for that reason. Ketchum's older, similar ADU rule has no long-term-rental alternative and offers no confirmed exemption, making its current enforceability genuinely uncertain.
operatingLimits: Ketchum's old one-STR-per-parcel cap and 2-night minimum appear to target STRs differently than ordinary homes and are very likely preempted, though this hasn't been formally confirmed in an adopted ordinance. No numeric cap was found in Sun Valley, Hailey, or Blaine County.

Taxes: state 8% baseline. Ketchum and Hailey both run a confirmed 4% local-option lodging tax (3% base + 1% supplemental) — roughly 12% combined in each — though a pending Hailey ballot measure may have already raised this to 6% (roughly 14% combined; outcome unconfirmed). Sun Valley confirms a 4% occupancy tax — also roughly 12% combined. Unincorporated Blaine County has no local-option tax — roughly 8% total, the lowest in the region.
investorNotes: Idaho's newer ADU-specific statute (§67-6541, from SB 1354) only bars owner-occupancy mandates in cities over 10,000 population — none of Ketchum, Sun Valley, or Hailey cross that threshold, so that particular law doesn't reach this region. The real protection against ADU owner-occupancy mandates here is the population-independent HB 583/§67-6539, which is almost certainly why Hailey rewrote its rule to add a long-term-rental alternative rather than drop the requirement outright.

Don't rely on Ketchum's own website for current STR rules — it appears to still describe a program the city may have already repealed. Confirm the actual adopted ordinance number and effective date directly with the city clerk.

Sun Valley's Elkhorn/Warm Springs condo complexes and various Ketchum condo buildings commonly carry private, pre-2022 minimum-stay/rental restrictions in their CC&Rs — these are grandfathered under Idaho Code §55-3211 and fully independent of the state's STR permit preemption.
Two local-option-tax ballot measures (Ketchum and possibly Hailey) may be pending or recently resolved — confirm current combined tax rates directly before quoting after-tax yields for this region.

sandpoint-pend-oreille.summary: Sandpoint's city council openly opposed HB 583 and used the full statutory three-readings process to delay compliance as long as legally possible, but the city's own site now confirms no general STR operating permit has been required since July 1, 2026 — its former 35-unit cap on non-owner-occupied STRs was already removed earlier that year. Unincorporated Bonner County is the opposite problem: its own live FAQ page still flatly states a Vacation Rental Permit is required, with no acknowledgment that the requirement is now preempted, creating real ambiguity about current enforcement in the Sagle/lake-shoreline area.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No general operating permit in Sandpoint as of July 1, 2026, per the city's own current page — only a separate Short-Term Rental Occupancy Tax Permit remains (for tax collection, not operating authority). Unincorporated Bonner County's own live FAQ still says flatly 'Vacation Rentals require a Vacation Rental Permit' with no HB 583 caveat — this permit is very likely legally unenforceable now, but the county's public materials give no indication of that; verify current practice directly (208-265-1458).

Primary residence required? No, in either jurisdiction — barred statewide, and Sandpoint's former 35-unit cap on non-owner-occupied STRs in residential zones was already removed via city Ordinance 1435 (effective Feb. 2026), before HB 583 even took effect.
operatingLimits: Sandpoint's former two-tier ordinary/high-occupancy system (with CUP-style review for 11+/12+ guest properties) is superseded by the city's own confirmation that no general permit applies at all. Bonner County's code still defines a separate High Occupancy Vacation Rental Permit (20+ occupants) and a base occupancy formula (2/bedroom+2, capped at 20) — the permit mechanism is very likely preempted, though the underlying occupancy math may survive as an IBC-adjacent standard.

Taxes: Sandpoint carries the highest confirmed combined tax rate found anywhere in this Idaho research — a 14% city Resort City Tax (two stacked 7% components, one from 2022) plus the 8% state baseline = 22% total inside city limits. Unincorporated Bonner County (including Sagle) has no local-option tax at all — just the 8% state baseline, a 14-point difference from in-town Sandpoint.
investorNotes: Sandpoint's council used a 3-2 first-reading vote (mayor breaking the tie) plus a unanimous 4-0 vote against expediting the process specifically to delay compliance as long as legally possible — a materially different (and more accurate) story than a simple '4-4 deadlock,' but the outcome is the same: full compliance as of July 1, 2026, per the city's own current page.

Bonner County's public materials have not been updated to reflect HB 583 at all — this is a real discrepancy between the law and what the county is telling the public, and a directly relevant diligence item for any Sagle-area or unincorporated-county property.

Idaho Code §55-3211 grandfathers pre-existing HOA rental restrictions on Lake Pend Oreille shoreline subdivisions in both Sandpoint and Sagle — check recorded CC&Rs directly, since these are unaffected by state or city deregulation.

The 22% total tax burden inside Sandpoint versus 8% in unincorporated Bonner County is a bigger swing than almost anywhere else in this research — confirm city-limits-vs-county status per parcel before modeling net yield.

lava-hot-springs.summary: Lava Hot Springs is the namesake city in the Idaho Supreme Court case that helped trigger statewide STR reform — the Court struck down its old zoning ban on non-owner-occupied rentals in May 2025, and the city's own May 2026 Ordinance 2026-005 replaced its prior regime with a pure health-and-safety ordinance containing no license, permit, fee, or owner-occupancy requirement at all. Unincorporated Bannock County has no STR-specific ordinance of any kind, so state law is essentially the whole story there.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No. Ordinance 2026-005 (adopted May 14, 2026) repeals the city's prior STR ordinance and contains no license, permit, registration, or fee requirement — a pure safety/occupancy ordinance consistent with what HB 583 still allows. No STR-specific permit or ordinance was found for unincorporated Bannock County at all.

Primary residence required? No — the Idaho Supreme Court already struck down the city's old owner-occupancy-based zoning distinction in May 2025, and HB 583 separately bars any owner-occupancy mandate statewide regardless.
operatingLimits: No caps or zoning exclusions remain in either jurisdiction. Occupancy is capped at International Building Code non-transient-residential limits (Ordinance 2026-005 §03.05.030(d)), tracking the state statute's own language almost verbatim. Required safety equipment: smoke alarms in every sleeping area, a fire extinguisher and CO detector per floor, removable escape ladders for above-ground sleeping rooms with windows, and a guest emergency-info handout.

Taxes: 8% state baseline, plus a city hotel-motel/STR occupancy tax reported at 3% — roughly 11% combined. The city has repeatedly (2021, and apparently again around 2024–2025) put a ballot measure to raise this to 5% before voters; no confirmed outcome was found, and independent 2026 sales-tax trackers still show the city's general rate unchanged, suggesting the increase likely hasn't passed — verify the current rate directly with Lava Hot Springs before publishing a number. No county-level lodging tax applies in unincorporated Bannock County.
investorNotes: The Idaho Assoc. of Realtors v. City of Lava Hot Springs Idaho Supreme Court ruling (May 2025) is specific to this city and holds that confining a whole category of STR (non-owner-occupied) to commercial zones is an unlawful practical prohibition, not a permissible 'regulation' — a favorable, on-point precedent unique to this region.

HB 583, passed roughly ten months after that ruling, went further and closed the licensing/fee workaround the ruling itself didn't address — the two are related but distinct legal developments, and Lava Hot Springs' Ordinance 2026-005 is the city's own direct response to HB 583 specifically, not the court case.

Lava is a tiny resort town (under ~400 year-round residents against roughly 400,000+ annual visitors) — its aggressive tourism-tax ballot history reflects genuine local fiscal pressure, worth knowing even though it hasn't yet translated into a higher confirmed rate.
Private HOA/CC&R restrictions were not identified for this region but would be unaffected by either the court ruling or HB 583 if any exist — check per property as with any Idaho market.

bear-lake.summary: Government-level STR rules on Idaho's side of Bear Lake are about as light as the law now allows — no county permit, cap, or owner-occupancy rule in Fish Haven, St. Charles, or the rest of unincorporated Bear Lake County. What keeps this region out of the top tier is a real, verified private restriction: the Bear Lake West subdivision's own governing documents ban STRs outright, a ban that predates Idaho's 2022 HOA-rental-restriction law and is confirmed still enforceable, plus a documented septic-capacity mismatch at some large group-hosting properties that state law doesn't address.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No — no countywide STR permit, license, or registration was found, and any such requirement would now be barred by HB 583 regardless. St. Charles, a small incorporated city, has no confirmed STR-specific rules either.

Primary residence required? No, government-wide. However, the Bear Lake West subdivision in Fish Haven (a substantial, amenity-rich HOA community with a golf course, restaurant, and HOA-managed water/sewer) bans short-term rentals outright in its own CC&Rs — confirmed directly from the HOA's own FAQ, and this predates Idaho's 2022 HOA-rental-restriction statute, so it's grandfathered and legally durable against current owners regardless of how permissive state law becomes.
operatingLimits: No occupancy cap or STR-specific inspection regime was found at the county level — a real soft spot, since local reporting documents some Idaho-side farmhouses hosting 60–80 guests against septic systems sized only by bedroom count (Idaho's statewide septic standard), not by actual advertised sleeping capacity. This is a structural mismatch state law doesn't address and isn't actively audited today.

Taxes: 8% state baseline only (6% sales + 2% Travel & Convention). No local-option or auditorium-district tax applies — unincorporated Fish Haven cannot levy one, and St. Charles doesn't appear on Idaho's resort-city local-option-tax list.
investorNotes: The Bear Lake West HOA ban is real and verified, not just alleged — the HOA's own governing-document language ('short term rentals or time shares is prohibited') was confirmed directly, and its president is on record explaining the ban predates the 2022 state HOA law specifically to survive it. This is a meaningfully different situation from most other 'Investor-Friendly' Idaho regions in this research, where the only friction is administrative lag, not a durable private ban.
HB 583/§67-6539 constrains only government regulation, not private HOA covenants — a property inside Bear Lake West cannot legally operate as an STR no matter how permissive county and state law are.

The septic-capacity/large-group-hosting gap is a real diligence and reputational-risk item on the Idaho side, and has drawn vocal local pushback (the Bear Lake Regional Commission's own director on record) that could eventually prompt the county to adopt the IBC-based occupancy limits it's currently entitled to but hasn't used.
No other named shorefront HOA was identified in this research — check parcel-level HOA membership before assuming any given Fish Haven or St. Charles listing is unrestricted.

garden-valley.summary: Neither Boise County nor the City of Crouch has ever adopted an STR-specific ordinance — there was nothing pre-HB-583 to repeal, and the incoming state preemption simply locks in that STRs must be treated as ordinary residential use going forward. The only real wrinkle is tax stacking: Crouch does levy a real, confirmed 3% lodging tax within its small city limits, a genuine surprise compared to the more common assumption that a town this size wouldn't bother.
permitResidency: Permit / license required? No, anywhere in this region — no STR-specific ordinance, permit, or license regime was found for unincorporated Boise County or the City of Crouch, past or present. Crouch does require a general, non-STR-specific $20/year Business/Vendor License for any commercial activity in city limits; how (or whether) this is applied to STR hosts in practice is unconfirmed.
Primary residence required? No — not required, and barred statewide regardless.
operatingLimits: No caps, density limits, or occupancy rules found at either the county or city level — standard IBC-based occupancy limits are the only ceiling that applies.

Taxes: 8% state baseline in unincorporated Garden Valley (the great majority of the region's inventory). Inside Crouch's small incorporated city limits specifically, a confirmed 3% room-occupancy Local Option Tax (voter-approved 2021, 66% in favor) applies on top — roughly 11% total there. The exact city-limits boundary could not be determined precisely; verify per-parcel via the Boise County Assessor GIS before assuming which rate applies.
investorNotes: This is a genuinely thin-documentation, sparsely-governed rural county (Boise County's own site is behind a bot-challenge, and Crouch is a town of ~150–200 people with a part-time city hall) — the surprising, well-confirmed finding is that Crouch does have a real, voter-approved lodging tax, contradicting the common assumption that a town this small wouldn't bother; everything else about the light-touch regulatory picture held up under deeper research.

Idaho Code §67-6539 bars STR-specific licenses, fees, permits, caps, and owner-occupancy mandates statewide — moot here in the sense that neither jurisdiction ever exercised that authority, but it forecloses either one from adopting such rules in the future.

It's unconfirmed whether Airbnb/Vrbo currently auto-collect Crouch's 3% local lodging tax on the city's behalf — hosts inside city limits should verify this directly with the platform and/or Crouch City Hall rather than assume.

South Fork Payette River subdivisions vary in HOA governance — some (e.g. Payette River Heights) are explicitly marketed as having no HOA/CC&Rs, while others (e.g. South Fork Landing, a PUD) likely carry HOA documents of unconfirmed STR content. Check per subdivision.
